questions.q: At a crossing of two straight lines, two vertically opposite angles together measure 130 degrees. Each of the other two angles measures ___ degrees.

Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: If two angles form a linear pair and one of them is 90 degrees, the other is also 90 degrees.
Statement 2: Vertically opposite angles always form a linear pair.
Statement 3: When two lines cross, it is possible for all four angles to be equal.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q: A crossing of two straight lines has one angle P of 37 degrees. One line is now turned about the crossing point so that P grows to 52 degrees. (a) What are the angle vertically opposite P and a neighbouring angle of P now? (b) By how many degrees did each of these two angles change, and what stays the same about every neighbouring pair?
questions.a: (a) The angle vertically opposite P is 52 degrees and a neighbour of P is 180 - 52 = 128 degrees. (b) The opposite angle rose by 15 (37 to 52) and the neighbour fell by 15 (143 to 128). Every neighbouring pair still adds to 180 degrees.
s: Part (a): 52 degrees for the vertically opposite angle and 128 degrees for the neighbour
Part (b): opposite angle up by 15, neighbour down by 15, neighbouring pairs still add to 180

questions.q: Two ways of studying a crossing of two lines are described. Method A: Zoya draws four pairs of crossing lines, measures the angles with a protractor and notices that vertically opposite angles come out equal. Method B: for an angle of 130 degrees she works out the linear-pair angle, and then the angle vertically opposite the 130 degree angle, using only the fact that a straight angle is 180 degrees. Compare the two methods: say what Method B gives for 130 degrees, why Method B holds for every crossing and Method A may not, and what the book calls Method B.
questions.a: Method B: the linear pair of 130 degrees is 50 degrees; the angle vertically opposite 130 degrees makes a linear pair with that 50 degree angle, so it is 180 - 50 = 130 degrees, equal to the first. Because only the 180 degree fact is used, never the size of the angle, the same steps work for any measure. Method A only checks the few drawings made, and each reading can be slightly off because of protractor use and line thickness. The book calls such a justification a proof.
s: Works out the linear pair 50 and the opposite angle 130 for Method B
Explains Method B never uses the size of the angle, so it holds for all crossings
Explains Method A checks only the drawings made and has measuring errors
Names Method B a proof

questions.q: Kabir's notebook says: 'Lines AB and CD cross at O and angle AOC = 70 degrees. Angle BOC is opposite to AOC, so BOC = 70 degrees. Angle BOD makes a linear pair with BOC, so BOD = 110 degrees. Angle AOD makes a linear pair with AOC, so AOD = 110 degrees.' Find his mistake, explain it, give the correct four angles and show that your four angles obey both rules of this section.
questions.a: Kabir's mistake: BOC is next to AOC (they share the arm OC and lie on the straight line AB), so they form a linear pair; BOC is not opposite to AOC. Correct angles: AOC = 70, BOC = 110, BOD = 70 (vertically opposite AOC), AOD = 110 (vertically opposite BOC, and also a linear pair with AOC). Check: each neighbouring pair adds to 180 (70 + 110) and each vertically opposite pair is equal (AOC = BOD, BOC = AOD).
s: Identifies that BOC is wrongly called opposite to AOC
Explains BOC and AOC are adjacent on straight line AB, a linear pair
Gives BOC = 110 degrees
Gives BOD = 70 and AOD = 110 degrees with reasons
Checks linear pairs add to 180 and opposite angles are equal

questions.q:
Gandhi Marg and Nehru Road are straight roads that cross at a chowk P. A bus bay can be built in a corner only if that corner measures at least 95 degrees; a bay built in a wrong corner would have to be dismantled at a cost of ₹6 lakh. Team A reads the north-east corner as 96 degrees and Team B reads the south-east corner as 86 degrees. Each reading is off from the true value by at most 1 degree.
(a) If Team B's reading were exact, what would the north-east corner be? (b) Between which two values does Team A's reading place the north-east corner? (c) Use both readings to find every value the north-east corner can have. (d) Should the council build the bay in the north-east corner? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The north-east and south-east corners form a linear pair, so the north-east corner would be 180 - 86 = 94 degrees. (b) From 95 to 97 degrees. (c) Team B's reading puts the south-east corner between 85 and 87, so the north-east corner (180 minus it) between 93 and 95. Only 95 lies in both ranges, so the north-east corner is exactly 95 degrees. (d) Yes. The only value consistent with both readings is 95, which meets the minimum of 'at least 95', so the bay will not have to be dismantled (the south-west corner, vertically opposite, is 95 too). Rejecting the corner because Team B's reading suggests 94 would ignore that Team B's reading is only good to 1 degree.
s: Part (a): 94 degrees from the linear pair
Part (b): 95 to 97 degrees
Part (c): intersects 95 to 97 with 93 to 95 and gets exactly 95
Part (d): decides to build because 95 is the only possible value and it meets the minimum

questions.q: Two bamboo sticks cross in a kite frame. Gita measures two neighbouring angles at the crossing as 68 and 112 degrees. Hari measures one angle as 68 degrees and the angle opposite it as 112 degrees. Whose readings can be right?
questions.a: Gita's only. Neighbouring angles form a linear pair and 68 + 112 = 180. Hari's opposite angles would have to be equal, and 68 is not 112.

questions.q:
Two straight lines cross. Match each situation in Column I with the measure in Column II.
Column I: I. Two vertically opposite angles together make 100 degrees: each of the other two angles   II. Two neighbouring angles at the crossing are equal: each   III. One angle of a linear pair is 40 degrees more than the other: the larger   IV. One angle is 35 degrees: the angle that forms a linear pair with its vertically opposite angle
Column II: A. 90 degrees   B. 110 degrees   C. 130 degrees   D. 145 degrees
questions.a: I-C, II-A, III-B, IV-D

questions.q: On a straight railway line, a branch line leaves at a junction and makes two angles with the main line. One angle is 40 degrees more than the other. What is the bigger angle?
questions.a: The two angles form a linear pair and add to 180. If the smaller is s, then s + (s + 40) = 180, so s = 70 and the bigger is 110 degrees. (70 is the smaller, 40 is the difference, 140 is 180 - 40.)

questions.q: True or False: Lines AB and CD cross at O and angle AOC is 70 degrees. Angles AOC and BOD form a linear pair, so angle BOD is 110 degrees. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Angles AOC and BOD lie directly across O, so they are vertically opposite, not a linear pair; they are equal and BOD is 70 degrees. The linear pairs of AOC are with COB and with AOD (110 degrees each).
s: Verdict False
Correction: AOC and BOD are vertically opposite and equal, BOD = 70 degrees

questions.q:
Hari, a welder in Nagpur, makes an X-shaped brace for a gate from two straight strips AB and CD crossing at O. With a protractor he reads: angle AOC 64 degrees, angle BOD 66 degrees, angle AOD 118 degrees and angle BOC 116 degrees. The design rule says every angle at the crossing must be at least 64 degrees. Each protractor reading can be off by up to 3 degrees. Re-welding the brace would cost ₹1,200; a careful re-measurement costs ₹100.
(a) Which readings should be equal, and which pairs should add up to 180 degrees? Say which pairs of Hari's readings break these rules. (b) The true angles obey AOC = BOD = T and AOD = BOC = 180 - T. Using the readings 64 and 66 only, between which values must T lie? (c) Now use all four readings: between which values must T lie? (d) Should Hari re-weld now? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Vertically opposite angles should be equal: AOC with BOD (64 and 66) and AOD with BOC (118 and 116) both differ. Neighbouring angles should add to 180: AOC + BOC = 180 is fine, but AOC + AOD = 182, BOD + AOD = 184 and BOD + BOC = 182 all fail. (b) T is within 3 of 64, so 61 to 67, and within 3 of 66, so 63 to 69: T lies from 63 to 67. (c) AOD = 180 - T is within 3 of 118, so T is from 59 to 65; BOC = 180 - T within 3 of 116, so T is from 61 to 67. With the earlier range, T lies from 63 to 65. (d) No, not yet. The true T could be 63, below the minimum of 64, or it could be 64 or 65, which pass; the readings cannot settle it. A ₹100 careful re-measurement is far cheaper than a ₹1,200 re-weld that may be unnecessary; re-weld only if the careful value is below 64.
s: Part (a): names the unequal opposite pairs and the three failing linear pairs
Part (b): gets T between 63 and 67
Part (c): gets T between 63 and 65 using all four readings
Part (d): says 63 would fail and 64 or 65 would pass, so re-measure for ₹100 before the ₹1,200 re-weld

questions.q: Karan measures the four angles around a crossing of two straight lines in order as 50 degrees, 120 degrees, 60 degrees and 130 degrees. Show that these readings cannot all be right.
questions.a: Neighbouring angles at the crossing form linear pairs and must add to 180 degrees, but 50 + 120 = 170, not 180. Opposite angles must be equal, but 50 is not 60 and 120 is not 130. So the readings cannot all be correct.
s: Tests a linear pair: 50 + 120 = 170, not 180
Tests vertically opposite angles: 50 is not 60 and 120 is not 130
Concludes the readings are impossible for two straight lines

questions.q: Rahul reads the four angles round a crossing of two straight lines, in order, as 61, 119, 63 and 117 degrees. Each reading can be off by at most 1 degree. Which set can be the true four angles, in the same order?
questions.a: 62, 118, 62, 118 is the only set in which opposite angles are equal and neighbours add to 180, and every reading is within 1 degree of it (61 to 62, 119 to 118, 63 to 62, 117 to 118). Sets starting 61 or 63 need a reading that is off by 2.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Vertically opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines are equal for every pair of lines.
Reason (R): On a drawing, protractor readings of two vertically opposite angles can differ by a degree or two because drawn lines have thickness.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Write expressions in x for two adjacent angles at the crossing of two straight lines such that x = 25 makes them a linear pair, and neither angle is 90 degrees. Check your answer.
questions.a: One answer: (4x + 20) degrees and (2x + 10) degrees. At x = 25 they are 120 and 60 degrees, which add to 180, and neither is 90. (Any pair of expressions that add to 180 at x = 25 and are not 90 each is accepted.)
s: Writes two expressions in x
Shows they add to 180 degrees when x = 25
Shows neither angle is 90 degrees

questions.q: The two blades of a pair of scissors are straight strips that cross at the pivot. When shut a little, the angle between the blades (on the tip side) is 28 degrees. The handles are the other ends of the same two strips. Find the angle between the handles. Then Rina opens the scissors so that the angle between the blades grows by 17 degrees: find the new angle between the handles and the new angle between a blade and a handle, and say how that last angle changed.
questions.a: The handles are on the other side of the pivot, so the angle between them is vertically opposite the blade angle: 28 degrees. After opening, the blade angle is 28 + 17 = 45 degrees and the handle angle is also 45 degrees. A blade and a handle make a linear pair with the blade angle, so that angle is 180 - 45 = 135 degrees; it was 180 - 28 = 152, so it fell by 17 degrees as the blade angle rose by 17.
s: Handle angle 28 degrees by vertical opposition
New blade and handle angles 45 and 45; blade-handle angle 135 degrees by a linear pair
Says the blade-handle angle fell from 152 to 135, by 17 degrees

questions.q: In a window grille, two straight bars cross. One angle at the crossing is 4z degrees and an adjacent angle, which forms a linear pair with it, is (2z + 30) degrees. What is the measure of the angle 4z?
questions.a: The linear pair adds to 180: 4z + 2z + 30 = 180, so z = 25 and 4z = 100 degrees. (60 comes from wrongly equating the two adjacent angles; 80 is the other angle; 25 is z itself.)

questions.q: At a crossing of two straight lines, angle p is 112 degrees. Maya says: 'The angle opposite p must be 68 degrees, because the two together make a straight line.' (a) Say what Maya has mixed up. (b) Give the angle vertically opposite p and the other two angles at the crossing.
questions.a: (a) Maya has treated vertically opposite angles like a linear pair. Two angles that make a straight line are neighbours (adjacent) and add to 180; angles across the crossing are equal. (b) The angle vertically opposite p is 112 degrees; the other two angles are each 180 - 112 = 68 degrees.
s: Part (a): says opposite angles are equal and it is the neighbours that add to 180
Part (b): 112 degrees opposite, and 68 and 68 for the other two

questions.q: Three straight lines pass through the same point O and make six angles. Going round O, the first three angles (one after the other) are (x + 10), (2x - 5) and (3x - 5) degrees, and each of the other three is vertically opposite one of these. (a) Explain why the first three angles add to 180 degrees and find x. (b) Write all six angles in order round O.
questions.a: (a) The first three angles together fill one side of a straight line, so they add to 180: (x + 10) + (2x - 5) + (3x - 5) = 6x = 180, so x = 30. (b) 40, 55, 85, 40, 55, 85 degrees (each of the last three is vertically opposite one of the first three).
s: Part (a): says the three angles lie on one side of a straight line, 6x = 180, x = 30

questions.q: Zoya wants to convince a friend that vertically opposite angles are equal even for an angle of 37.5 degrees that nobody has measured. Which argument works for every possible angle?
o: Each is a linear pair with the same neighbour, so each is 180 minus it
Measure a great many more crossings with a protractor until no pair differs
Both open out from the same line, so their readings must agree anyway
They lie on opposite sides of the point, so one mirrors the other exactly
questions.a: Both vertically opposite angles make a linear pair with the same neighbour, so each is 180 minus it and they are equal for any value. Measuring cannot cover every angle.

questions.q: Tara draws a straight line AB with a point O on it and a ray OC, so that angle AOC is (2a + 10) degrees and angle COB is (3a - 20) degrees. She then extends CO backwards to D so that CD is a straight line. (a) Find a and the two angles. (b) Find angle AOD and angle BOD.
questions.a: (a) 2a + 10 + 3a - 20 = 180, so a = 38; AOC = 86 degrees and COB = 94 degrees. (b) AOD is vertically opposite COB, so 94 degrees; BOD is vertically opposite AOC, so 86 degrees.
s: Part (a): a = 38, angles 86 and 94 degrees
Part (b): AOD = 94 and BOD = 86 by vertical opposition

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If a linear pair consists of two equal angles, each of the angles measures 90 degrees.
Reason (R): The two angles of a linear pair add up to 180 degrees.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: Rina measures only one of the four angles at the crossing of lines AB and CD and finds it is 90 degrees. She says she need not measure the other three, because the lines are already known to be perpendicular. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. One angle of 90 degrees gives a linear-pair angle of 180 - 90 = 90 degrees on either side and a vertically opposite angle of 90 degrees, so all four angles are 90 degrees and the lines are perpendicular. Nothing more needs measuring.
s: Verdict True
Reason: the other three follow from linear pairs and vertically opposite angles

questions.q: A carpenter checks whether a table leg is perpendicular to the top, where the leg and the top edge are straight. She reads the four angles round the joint, in order, as 88, 93, 87 and 92 degrees. Each protractor reading is off from the true value by at most 2 degrees. The true angles obey: the first and third are equal to T, and the second and fourth are each 180 - T. Between which values must T lie if she uses only the first reading? Using all four readings? Can she say the leg is perpendicular, and why does using all four readings help?
questions.a: First reading only: T lies from 88 - 2 = 86 to 88 + 2 = 90, so 90 (perpendicular) cannot be ruled out. All four: the first and third readings give T from 86 to 90 and from 85 to 89, so 86 to 89; the second gives 180 - T from 91 to 95, so T from 85 to 89; the fourth gives T from 86 to 90. Together T lies from 86 to 89. Since T is less than 90, the leg is not perpendicular; it is off by at least 1 degree. Using all four readings narrows the range because each reading says something about the same T through the two rules, and here they push the upper limit below 90.
s: T from 86 to 90 using the first reading alone, so 90 is not ruled out
Converts the second and fourth readings to ranges for T (85 to 89 and 86 to 90)
Intersects all four ranges to get T from 86 to 89
Concludes the leg is not perpendicular, off by at least 1 degree
Explains the equal and 180 rules let every reading restrict the same T

questions.q: Lines AB and CD cross at O. A surveyor reports that angle AOC and angle BOD add up to 180 degrees. What can be concluded?
questions.a: Angles AOC and BOD are vertically opposite, so they are equal; equal angles adding to 180 are 90 degrees each. So the lines are perpendicular.
o: The lines are perpendicular, since AOC = BOD = 90 degrees
The lines are parallel, since the angles add to 180 degrees
Nothing special, since AOC and BOD always add to 180 degrees
AOC and BOD form a linear pair, so they can have any values

questions.q:
An architect draws three plans for a house in Indore. In each, a straight wall AB is crossed at O by a straight corridor wall CD. In Plan 1, angle AOC is 89 degrees and the plan costs ₹2.1 lakh. In Plan 2, angle AOC is 90 degrees and the plan costs ₹2.6 lakh. In Plan 3, angle AOC is 86 degrees and the plan costs ₹2.0 lakh. The cupboards fit if the corridor is within 2 degrees of perpendicular to AB. The owner also wants a sliding door at O, which fits only if the corridor is exactly perpendicular; making a plan exactly perpendicular afterwards costs ₹0.7 lakh extra, for any plan. She will pay at most ₹0.4 lakh above the cheapest cupboard-friendly plan to have the sliding door.
(a) Find angle AOD in Plan 1. (b) By how many degrees does each plan differ from a right angle? (c) Which plans suit the cupboards without any change? (d) Which plan should she choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Angle AOD forms a linear pair with angle AOC: 180 - 89 = 91 degrees. (b) Plan 1: 1 degree, Plan 2: 0 degrees, Plan 3: 4 degrees. (c) Plans 1 and 2 (within 2 degrees); Plan 3 is 4 degrees off. (d) Plan 1. The cheapest cupboard-friendly plan is Plan 1 at ₹2.1 lakh. The cheapest way to get the sliding door is Plan 2 at ₹2.6 lakh (Plan 1 fixed costs 2.1 + 0.7 = ₹2.8 lakh, Plan 3 fixed costs 2.0 + 0.7 = ₹2.7 lakh). The door costs 2.6 - 2.1 = ₹0.5 lakh extra, which is above her limit of ₹0.4 lakh, so she should take Plan 1 and do without the door.
s: Part (a): gets 91 degrees using a linear pair
Part (b): gives 1, 0 and 4 degrees
Part (c): picks Plans 1 and 2
Part (d): finds the door route costs ₹2.6 lakh (Plan 2) against ₹2.1 lakh, so 0.5 lakh extra exceeds 0.4, and picks Plan 1

questions.q: Lines AB and CD are perpendicular and cross at O. A third line EF passes through O with E inside angle AOC, so that angle AOE is 35 degrees. (a) Find angle EOC and angle EOD. (b) Is EF perpendicular to CD? Use your answers to decide.
questions.a: (a) Angle AOC is 90 degrees, so EOC = 90 - 35 = 55 degrees. C, O, D lie on a straight line, so EOD = 180 - 55 = 125 degrees. (b) No. The angles EF makes with CD are 55 and 125 degrees; a perpendicular line would make 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): EOC = 55 degrees and EOD = 125 degrees
Part (b): says not perpendicular, since 55 and 125 are not 90

questions.q:
For Sports Day at a school in Coimbatore, the groundsman chalks a centre line PQ and a boundary line RS across a field. They cross at O. He checks one corner with a wooden set square and finds that angle POR fits the 90 degree corner of the set square exactly. His assistant then reads angle QOS on a protractor as 3k degrees. The two angles are vertically opposite.
(a) What are the relationship of lines PQ and RS and the measure of angle ROQ? (b) Find k. (c) Which mark should the plan carry at O? (d) The assistant suggests measuring all four angles with a protractor on the thick chalk lines. The groundsman prefers one set-square check. Which is enough to prove the lines perpendicular, and which would you trust more? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The set square fits angle POR exactly, so it is 90 degrees and the lines are perpendicular; angle ROQ forms a linear pair with it, so it is 90 degrees. (b) Angle QOS equals the vertically opposite angle POR = 90, so 3k = 90 and k = 30. (c) A small square at O. (d) One right angle is enough, because the other three follow from linear pairs and vertically opposite angles; the set square is more reliable, as protractor readings on thick chalk lines can be a degree or two off.
s: Part (a): says perpendicular and angle ROQ = 90 degrees
Part (b): equates 3k to the vertically opposite 90 degrees and gets k = 30
Part (c): names the square mark
Part (d): says one check suffices and trusts the set square because of measurement error

questions.q: At the crossing of two straight lines, the angles a, b, c, d are named in order round the point, and a surveyor finds that a = b. Which statement must then be true?
questions.a: Equal adjacent angles are 90 degrees each, so all four angles are 90 and a + c = 180 degrees. The other sums would need the angles to be 45 or 135 degrees.

questions.q: Lines AB and CD cross at O. Angle AOC is (4y - 20) degrees and the neighbouring angle BOC is (2y + 50) degrees. Suchi finds y by setting the two angles equal. Dev finds y by adding them to 180. Which method is right for these two angles, and why? Use it to find y and both angles, and say whether the lines are perpendicular.
questions.a: Angles AOC and BOC are neighbours on the straight line AB, so they form a linear pair and add to 180; nothing says they are equal, so Dev's method is right. (4y - 20) + (2y + 50) = 6y + 30 = 180, so y = 25; AOC = 80 degrees and BOC = 100 degrees. They are not equal, so the lines are not perpendicular. (Suchi's method gives y = 35 and 120 + 120 = 240, which is not 180.)
s: Says AOC and BOC are a linear pair, so they add to 180 (Dev's method)
Gets y = 25, AOC = 80 and BOC = 100 degrees
Concludes not perpendicular, since 80 is not 100; Suchi's 120 and 120 do not add to 180

questions.q: A student writes: 'If one of the four angles at a crossing is 90 degrees, the lines are perpendicular. The other two angles are also 90 degrees because they are vertically opposite to the 90 degree angles.' Is this correct?
questions.a: Partly right. A 90 degree angle does make the lines perpendicular, and its vertically opposite angle is 90 degrees. But the other two angles are not vertically opposite to the 90 degree angles; each forms a linear pair with one (180 - 90 = 90). So the conclusion is right and the reason is wrong.
s: Says the claim is only partly correct
Accepts that one 90 degree angle gives perpendicular lines
Corrects the reason: the other two angles are 90 by linear pair, not vertically opposite

questions.q: Show that two straight lines cannot cross so that three of the four angles are 90 degrees and the fourth is 80 degrees.
questions.a: The angle of 80 degrees would form a linear pair with a 90 degree angle, so the two would add to 170 degrees, but a linear pair must add to 180 degrees. Also it would be opposite another 90 degree angle, and vertically opposite angles must be equal. So it cannot happen.
s: Tests the linear pair 90 + 80 = 170, not 180
Uses vertically opposite angles must be equal (80 is not 90)
Concludes it is impossible

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: Two crossing lines are perpendicular only if the two lines are equally long.
Statement 2: If two intersecting lines make one right angle, they make four right angles.
Statement 3: Perpendicular lines are marked with a double arrow.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only

questions.q: Lines AB and CD are perpendicular and cross at O. A ray OE inside angle AOC is drawn so that it cuts angle AOC into two equal parts. (a) Find angle AOE and angle COE. (b) Find angle BOE and angle DOE, and say whether OE is perpendicular to AB or to CD.
questions.a: (a) Angle AOC is 90 degrees, so AOE = COE = 45 degrees. (b) A, O, B lie on a straight line, so BOE = 180 - 45 = 135 degrees; C, O, D lie on a straight line, so DOE = 180 - 45 = 135 degrees. OE is not perpendicular to either line, since none of its angles with AB or CD is 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): 45 degrees and 45 degrees
Part (b): 135 and 135 degrees by linear pairs, and OE is perpendicular to neither line

questions.q: At the crossing of two railway lines, two adjacent angles measure (2m + 20) degrees and (3m - 15) degrees, and the surveyor finds them equal. What are m and the relation of the lines?
o: m = 35, and the lines are perpendicular
m = 35, and the lines are parallel
m = 37, and the lines are perpendicular
m = 70, and the lines are perpendicular
questions.a: Equal adjacent angles form a linear pair, so 2m + 20 = 3m - 15 gives m = 35 (also 5m + 5 = 180 gives 5m = 175, m = 35). Each angle is 90 degrees, so the lines are perpendicular. Parallel lines do not cross at all. (37 comes from 5m + 5 = 185 divided by 5; 70 is double m.)

questions.q: At the crossing of lines AB and CD, angle AOC is (2x + 10) degrees and the angle vertically opposite it, angle BOD, is (4x - 10) degrees. Adnan says the lines must be perpendicular because 'two equal angles at a crossing mean 90 degrees'. (a) Find x and angle AOC. (b) Is Adnan right? Find angle AOD and decide.
questions.a: (a) Vertically opposite angles are equal, so 2x + 10 = 4x - 10, x = 10, and angle AOC = 30 degrees. (b) No. AOD forms a linear pair with AOC, so AOD = 180 - 30 = 150 degrees. The lines are not perpendicular. Equal adjacent angles (a linear pair) would give 90 degrees; vertically opposite angles are always equal and say nothing about 90.
s: Part (a): sets 2x + 10 = 4x - 10, x = 10, AOC = 30 degrees
Part (b): finds AOD = 150 and says not perpendicular, since equal opposite angles do not force 90 degrees

questions.q: A diagram has four lines. Lines p and q carry one arrow mark each, lines r and s carry two arrow marks each, and a small square is drawn at the crossing of p and r. How many pairs of lines does the diagram mark as parallel, and how many as perpendicular?
questions.a: p and q form one marked parallel pair and r and s form another, so 2 parallel pairs. The square marks only p and r, so 1 marked perpendicular pair.

questions.q: Lines AB and CD cross at O. Five students each try to prove that AB is perpendicular to CD from a single fact. Ravi: angle AOC is 90 degrees. Sita: angle AOC equals angle BOD. Tej: angle AOC equals angle AOD. Uma: angle AOC and angle BOD add up to 180 degrees. Vimal: angle AOC and angle AOD add up to 180 degrees. For each student say whether the fact proves the lines perpendicular, and give the reason.
questions.a: Ravi: yes, the angle is a right angle. Sita: no, vertically opposite angles are always equal, so this holds for every crossing (for example 70, 110, 70, 110). Tej: yes, AOC and AOD are a linear pair, so equal angles are 180 / 2 = 90 degrees each. Uma: yes, AOC and BOD are vertically opposite, so equal, and equal angles adding to 180 are 90 each. Vimal: no, AOC and AOD are a linear pair, so they always add to 180 whatever the angle.
s: Ravi: yes, with the reason
Sita: no, because vertically opposite angles are always equal
Tej: yes, equal linear pair gives 90
Uma: yes, equal opposite angles adding to 180 give 90
Vimal: no, a linear pair always adds to 180

questions.q: A surveyor lists the four angles round the crossing of two straight roads, in order, for four junctions. Junction 1: 90, 90, 90, 90. Junction 2: 80, 100, 80, 100. Junction 3: 90, 90, 80, 100. Junction 4: 85, 95, 85, 95. (a) At which junctions are the roads perpendicular? (b) One junction's list cannot be right for two straight roads; name it and say which rule it breaks.
questions.a: (a) Only junction 1 (all four angles are 90 degrees). Junctions 2 and 4 are valid crossings but have angles other than 90. (b) Junction 3: its third angle (80) is opposite the first (90), but vertically opposite angles must be equal; also its second and third angles are neighbours and 90 + 80 = 170, not 180.
s: Part (a): junction 1 only
Part (b): names junction 3 and the broken rule (opposite angles unequal or linear pair not 180)

questions.q: Meera folds a rectangular sheet in half from top to bottom, opens it, then folds it in half from left to right and opens it again. The two creases cross at the centre O. Which statement about the opened sheet is correct?
questions.a: The two creases make 4 right angles at O, and the top-to-bottom crease is parallel to the top edge. (The fold puts the top edge on the bottom edge, so that crease runs the same way as the top edge and across the left edge.)
o: The creases make 4 right angles at O, and the top-to-bottom crease is parallel to the top edge
The creases make 4 right angles at O, and the top-to-bottom crease is parallel to the left edge
The creases make 2 right angles at O, and the top-to-bottom crease is parallel to the top edge
The creases make 2 right angles at O, and the top-to-bottom crease is parallel to the left edge

questions.q: At a crossing of two straight lines, three of the four angles are equal. Each of the four angles measures ___ degrees.

A transversal l cuts lines m and n at X and Y. The upper-right angle at X on m is 75 degrees. The lower-right angle at Y on n is 105 degrees. Both are exact. Faiz says m and n are not parallel because 75 and 105 are unequal. Priya says they are parallel. Who is right? Give the reason.
questions.a: Priya is right. Faiz compared angles in different positions. The lower-right angle at Y forms a linear pair with the upper-right angle at Y, so the upper-right angle at Y is 180 - 105 = 75 degrees. The corresponding angles at X and Y are 75 and 75, equal, so m and n are parallel.
s: Picks Priya
Says Faiz compared angles in different positions and finds the upper-right angle at Y is 75 by a linear pair
Concludes equal corresponding angles, so parallel

questions.q: A transversal cuts lines a and b. Meena reads the upper-left angles as 62 degrees at a and 62 degrees at b, and the upper-right angles as 118 degrees at a and 120 degrees at b. Show that these four readings cannot all be exact.
questions.a: At each line the upper-left and upper-right angles lie on the straight line, so they form a linear pair and add to 180. At a: 62 + 118 = 180, which is fine. At b: 62 + 120 = 182, not 180. So the four readings cannot all be exact; at least one reading at b is wrong.
s: Says upper-left and upper-right at one line form a linear pair adding to 180
Concludes the readings cannot all be exact

questions.q: Rohan wants to show that sides PS and QR of a rectangle PQRS are parallel. In the rectangle PQ is the bottom side, S is above P, R is above Q, and T lies on PQ extended to the right of Q. He writes: 'Angle SPQ and angle RQP are both 90 degrees, so they are equal corresponding angles, and PS is parallel to QR.' Is his argument correct? Explain what is wrong, then repair it by extending PQ beyond Q to a point T: find the angle that really corresponds to angle SPQ, give its measure with a reason, and state the conclusion. Say how you would show that PQ is parallel to SR.
questions.a: Rohan's angles SPQ and RQP lie between the lines PS and QR on the same side of PQ; they are interior angles on the same side, not corresponding angles, and the book proves parallel lines only from equal corresponding angles. The angle that corresponds to angle SPQ is angle RQT at Q, above PQ and on the right. Angle RQT forms a linear pair with angle RQP, so it is 180 - 90 = 90 degrees. Corresponding angles SPQ and RQT are equal (90 and 90), so PS is parallel to QR. In the same way, extending PS beyond S and using PS as the transversal, the corresponding angles at P and at S are equal, so PQ is parallel to SR.
s: Says SPQ and RQP are not corresponding angles
Identifies angle RQT as the corresponding angle of SPQ
Shows angle RQT is 90 degrees by a linear pair with RQP
Concludes PS is parallel to QR from equal corresponding angles
Says the same method with another transversal and extension shows PQ is parallel to SR

questions.q: A transversal cuts line l and line m. At l a corresponding angle is 65 degrees, and the matching corresponding angle at m is (2x + 5) degrees. For l and m to be parallel, what must x be?
questions.a: Parallel lines need equal corresponding angles: 2x + 5 = 65, so x = 30. (55 uses the linear-pair angle 115 by mistake; 32.5 and 57.5 forget the +5.)

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: Two lines on a flat page that do not meet anywhere inside the page are parallel.
Statement 2: In a figure where three lines carry one arrow mark and two lines carry two arrow marks, there are two sets of parallel lines.
Statement 3: Two lines drawn with a set square, both at 90 degrees to a line l, are parallel.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two lines on a sheet of paper that do not meet inside the sheet are always parallel.
Reason (R): Parallel lines do not meet however far they are extended at both ends.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: A transversal t crosses line l at X so that the upper-right angle at X is 66 degrees. Sneha wants a line m through a point Y of t that is parallel to l. By mistake she marks 66 degrees as the lower-right angle at Y and draws m. (a) What is the upper-right angle at Y on her line m? (b) Is m parallel to l? How should she correct the line?
questions.a: (a) The upper-right and lower-right angles at Y form a linear pair along t, so the upper-right angle is 180 - 66 = 114 degrees. (b) No: the corresponding angles are 66 at X and 114 at Y, which are unequal. She should draw m so that the upper-right angle at Y is 66 degrees (the lower-right angle then 114).
s: Part (a): 114 degrees by a linear pair
Part (b): not parallel since 66 is not 114, and the upper-right angle at Y must be 66

questions.q: Four students each test a different pair of inked lines on a metal sheet with one transversal and exact readings. Ali: the upper-right angle at the first line is 68 degrees and the upper-left angle at the second line is 112 degrees. Bina: the lower-left angles at both lines are 112 degrees. Chetan: the upper-right angle at the first line is 68 degrees and the lower-right angle at the second line is 68 degrees. Dev: the lower-left angle at the first line is 68 degrees and the upper-right angle at the second line is 68 degrees. For each student say whether the lines are parallel, and give the step that decides it.
questions.a: Ali: parallel; the upper-right angle at the second line is 180 - 112 = 68, equal to the first line's upper-right angle. Bina: parallel; the lower-left angles are in the same position, 112 and 112, so corresponding angles are equal. Chetan: not parallel; the lower-right angle 68 gives an upper-right angle of 180 - 68 = 112 at the second line, which is not equal to 68. Dev: parallel; the lower-left angle at the first line is vertically opposite its upper-right angle, so that angle is 68 degrees, equal to the upper-right angle 68 at the second line.
s: Ali: parallel, with the linear pair step
Bina: parallel, since the corresponding angles are equal as read
Chetan: not parallel, with the step to 112 against 68
Dev: parallel, using vertical opposition to get 68 at the first line
States that angles must be brought to the same position before they are compared

questions.q:
Ramesh, a carpenter in Jaipur, is fitting a ladder with two side rails PQ and RS. Rung 1, XY, joins X on PQ to Y on RS. He measures the angle below PQ and to the left of the rung at X, and the angle below RS and to the left of the rung at Y: 72 degrees and 72 degrees. Rung 2, X1Y1, gives the same-position readings 72 degrees at X1 and 70 degrees at Y1. His protractor readings can each be off by at most 1 degree.
(a) Which kind of angles are these? (b) If rung 1's readings were exact, what would that say about the rails? (c) If rung 2's readings were exact, what would that say about the rails? (d) Can the true corresponding angles of all three readings be equal? Decide whether the readings show the rails are not parallel.
questions.a: (a) Corresponding angles. (b) The rails would be parallel, since the corresponding angles are equal. (c) The rails would not be parallel, since 72 and 70 are unequal. (d) Yes. If the true corresponding angle is 71 degrees on both rails, each reading (72, 72, 72 and 70) is within 1 degree of it. So the data are consistent with parallel rails and do not show that the rails are not parallel; Ramesh has no evidence against parallel rails from these readings.
s: Part (a): names corresponding angles
Part (b): says parallel from 72 = 72
Part (c): says not parallel from 72 and 70
Part (d): shows 71 is within 1 degree of every reading, so parallel rails fit, and the readings do not prove the rails are not parallel

questions.q: Anu keeps a ruler flat and places the slanting edge of a set square so that it makes 58 degrees with the ruler, on the upper-right of the point where the edge meets the ruler. She draws a line l along the edge, slides the set square along the ruler and draws a second line m along the same edge. Where m meets the ruler, the lower-right angle (between m and the ruler) is ___ degrees.

True or False: When Kavya folds a crease t through A perpendicular to l and then a crease m through A perpendicular to t, the crease m is parallel to l only because both creases pass through the same point A. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The point A does not make them parallel. Both l and m make a right angle with the transversal t, so the corresponding angles are equal (90 degrees each), and that is why l and m are parallel.
s: Verdict False
Reason: equal corresponding angles of 90 degrees with t, not the common point

questions.q: A transversal t cuts lines l and m. At l the upper-right angle is 68 degrees. At m the upper-left angle is 112 degrees. Aman compares 68 with 112, finds them unequal and says l and m are not parallel. (a) What is wrong with Aman's comparison? (b) Give the correct conclusion with a reason.
questions.a: (a) The upper-right angle at l and the upper-left angle at m are not in the same position, so they are not corresponding angles; equal corresponding angles are needed for the test. (b) The upper-left angle at m is 112 degrees, so the upper-right angle at m forms a linear pair with it: 180 - 112 = 68 degrees. The corresponding angles (upper-right at l and at m) are 68 and 68, equal, so l and m are parallel.
s: Part (a): the two angles are in different positions, not corresponding
Part (b): finds the upper-right angle at m is 68, equal to that at l, so parallel

questions.q: On dot paper Divya cannot tell by eye which of lines b and c is parallel to line a. She cuts all three with a transversal and measures exactly the upper-right angles: 52 degrees at a, 52 degrees at b and 58 degrees at c. (a) Which of b and c is parallel to a? (b) Divya says that line c would pass the test if she measured the lower-left angles instead. Check this using the lower-left angles.
questions.a: (a) Line b, because its corresponding angle (52) equals that at a; c has 58, which is different. (b) The lower-left angles are vertically opposite the upper-right angles, so they are 52 at a and 58 at c. These are again unequal, so c still fails; the other pair of corresponding angles cannot rescue it.
s: Part (a): picks b since 52 = 52 and 52 is not 58
Part (b): shows the lower-left angles are 52 and 58, still unequal

questions.q: Write a set of two readings that shows lines m and n are parallel, in which the two angles you measured are NOT in the same position and have different numbers. A transversal crosses m at X and n at Y; the upper-right angle at X is 70 degrees. Give the second reading (position and measure) and show how the corresponding angles prove m is parallel to n.
questions.a: One answer: the lower-right angle at Y is 110 degrees. The upper-right angle at Y forms a linear pair with it, so it is 180 - 110 = 70 degrees. The corresponding angles (both upper-right) are 70 and 70, equal, so m is parallel to n. (Any position and value that leads to 70 in the upper-right position at Y is accepted, for example the upper-left angle 110 or the lower-left angle 70.)
s: Gives a second reading in a different position with a different number
Converts it to the upper-right angle at Y, 70 degrees
Concludes the corresponding angles are equal, so m is parallel to n

questions.q: Lines p, q and r are cut by one transversal. Lines p and q are known to be parallel. The corresponding angles at q and at r are equal. What can be said about p and r?
questions.a: Because p and q are parallel, the corresponding angles at p and q are equal; those at q and r are equal too, so the angles at p and r are equal and p and r are parallel.
o: p and r are parallel, since all three corresponding angles are equal
p and r are not parallel, because only q was compared with each of them
Nothing can be said until a second transversal is drawn across p and r
p and r are perpendicular, since q is parallel to p

questions.q: Mahi draws lines p and q on a notebook page and they do not meet inside the page. She extends both with a ruler on a long sheet and they cross 60 cm beyond the page. Another pair, r and s, are followed for 3 m on a hall floor without meeting. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.a: p and q meet, so they are not parallel (parallel lines never meet however far extended). For r and s, 3 m of not meeting does not show that they never meet, so nothing is settled.
o: p and q are not parallel, and nothing is yet settled about r and s
p and q are parallel because they did not meet on the page, and so are r and s
p and q are not parallel, and r and s are parallel because they did not meet
Neither pair can be parallel, because lines on paper always meet when extended

questions.q: A figure has five lines a, b, c, d and e. Lines a, c and e carry one arrow mark each, and lines b and d carry two arrow marks each. (a) Which lines are declared parallel to line c? (b) A sixth line f is added and declared parallel to b. Which lines are now parallel to d, and how many arrow marks must f carry?
questions.a: (a) The lines with the same number of arrows as c: a and e. (b) Lines parallel to d are b and now f; f must carry two arrow marks, the same as b and d.
s: Part (a): a and e
Part (b): b and f are parallel to d, and f has two arrow marks

questions.q: Lines a and b are cut by a transversal t, and the corresponding angles at the two lines are 65 degrees and 65 degrees. A second transversal s is drawn across the same lines and is slanted differently. What can be said about the corresponding angles made by s?
questions.a: Since the corresponding angles with t are equal, a and b are parallel. For parallel lines every transversal gives equal corresponding angles, so s makes equal corresponding angles too, but they need not be 65 degrees because s has a different slant.
o: They are equal to each other, but not necessarily 65 degrees
They need not be equal to each other

questions.q: Vikram cuts two lines p and q with a transversal. The upper-left angle at p is 62 degrees and the upper-right angle at q is 118 degrees. A friend says p and q are parallel. Is the friend right?
questions.a: Yes. The upper-right angle at p forms a linear pair with the 62 degree upper-left angle, so it is 118 degrees. It corresponds to the upper-right angle at q (118 degrees), and equal corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel.
o: Yes: the upper-right angle at p is 118 degrees, equal to the one at q
No: 62 and 118 are unequal, so the lines are not parallel
No: 62 and 118 add to 180, which shows the lines meet
Yes: the two angles add to 180 degrees, so they are corresponding

questions.q:
Aditi draws a line l. With the 45 degree corner of her set square she draws four lines a, b, c and d through different points of l. For each she measures the angle above l, on the right of the point where it crosses l: a gives 45 degrees, b gives 45 degrees, c gives 135 degrees and d gives 47 degrees. For hand-drawn lines she accepts a difference of up to 1 degree. She has time to redraw only one line before the exhibition, and she wants as many lines as possible to be parallel with the smallest remaining error.
(a) What type of angles are these, and which line is parallel to a? (b) Why is c not parallel to a? (c) Is d parallel to a within her limit? (d) Which line should she redraw, and at what angle? Compare the two choices c and d by the largest error left.
questions.a: (a) They are corresponding angles with l as the transversal; b is parallel to a (45 and 45). (b) The corresponding angles are 45 and 135, which are not equal. (c) No; 47 differs from 45 by 2 degrees, which is more than her limit of 1 degree. (d) She should redraw c at 45 degrees. Redrawing c leaves a, b and c parallel and the largest error left is 2 degrees (line d). Redrawing d instead leaves a, b and d parallel but line c stays 90 degrees (135 - 45) off. So redraw c.
s: Part (a): corresponding angles and b parallel to a
Part (b): 45 is not 135
Part (c): 47 is 2 degrees from 45, outside the 1 degree limit
Part (d): redraw c at 45, comparing the leftover errors 2 degrees against 90 degrees

questions.q: Transversal t crosses line l at P and line m at Q, with m below l. Around P the angles are 1 (upper-left), 2 (upper-right), 3 (lower-right) and 4 (lower-left). Around Q the angles are 5 (upper-left), 6 (upper-right), 7 (lower-right) and 8 (lower-left). Lines l and m are parallel and angle 2 is 70 degrees. (a) Which angles at P can be found without using that the lines are parallel? Give their measures. (b) Which angle at Q is the corresponding angle of angle 2 (this is the one step that needs the parallel fact)? Then give the other three angles at Q using only linear pairs and vertically opposite angles.
questions.a: (a) Angle 1 and angle 3 each form a linear pair with angle 2, so they are 110 degrees; angle 4 is vertically opposite angle 2, so it is 70 degrees. (b) Angle 6 is the corresponding angle of angle 2, so it is 70 degrees. Then angles 5 and 7 are 110 degrees each (linear pairs with angle 6) and angle 8 is 70 degrees (vertically opposite angle 6).
s: Part (a): gives angles 1 and 3 as 110 degrees and angle 4 as 70 degrees
Part (b): names angle 6 as the corresponding angle (70 degrees) and gives 5 and 7 as 110 degrees, 8 as 70 degrees

questions.q: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. The upper-left angle at the first line is (3a - 10) degrees and the lower-right angle at the second line is (2a + 25) degrees. What is a?
questions.a: The upper-left angle at the first line corresponds to the upper-left angle at the second line, which is vertically opposite the lower-right angle there. So the two given angles are equal: 3a - 10 = 2a + 25 and a = 35 (both are 95 degrees). (33 comes from wrongly adding them to 180; 15 from 3a + 10.)

questions.q: Transversal t crosses line l at P and line m at Q, with m below l. Around P the angles are 1 (upper-left), 2 (upper-right), 3 (lower-right) and 4 (lower-left). Around Q the angles are 5 (upper-left), 6 (upper-right), 7 (lower-right) and 8 (lower-left). Lines l and m are parallel and angle 1 is 105 degrees. Aman says angle 1 and angle 7 are corresponding angles, because they are diagonally across from each other. (a) Correct his naming. (b) Find angle 7 and angle 6, and say which of the two is equal to angle 1.
questions.a: (a) Angle 1 is upper-left at P and angle 7 is lower-right at Q. Corresponding angles must be in the same position, so angle 1 corresponds to angle 5, not to angle 7. (b) Angle 5 = 105 degrees (corresponding to angle 1). Angle 7 is vertically opposite angle 5, so it is 105 degrees, equal to angle 1. Angle 6 forms a linear pair with angle 5, so it is 75 degrees. His naming was wrong although angle 7 does equal angle 1.
s: Part (a): angle 1 corresponds to angle 5, since angle 7 is in a different position
Part (b): angle 7 = 105 degrees (equal to angle 1) and angle 6 = 75 degrees

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: A transversal on two lines forms eight angles, and all eight can always be different.
Statement 2: The eight angles formed by a transversal make four pairs of vertically opposite angles, equal in each pair.
Statement 3: It is possible to draw a transversal on two lines so that only two different angle measures appear.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q: A transversal cuts two parallel lines l and m, and one of the eight angles measures 65 degrees. The sum of all eight angles is ___ degrees.

For the annual day stage at a school in Hyderabad, an electrician reports the angles made where a pipe t crosses two stage pipes l and m. He lists them in the order upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, lower-left. At l: 70, 110, 70, 110 degrees. At m: 72, 108, 80, 100 degrees. He read the upper two angles at m and all four at l directly with a set square, which is good to within 3 degrees; the lower two at m were worked out in a hurry. The stage manager's rule is to approve pipes as parallel only if the directly read corresponding angles differ by at most 1 degree; otherwise she orders a fresh inspection, which costs ₹1,500 and a day. If the pipes are not parallel the backdrop hangs crooked and has to be redone at a cost of ₹30,000.
(a) Which two readings at m break the rules for the angles at a crossing? (b) What should they be? (c) How many different measures are in the corrected list of all eight angles? (d) Should the manager approve the pipes as parallel now or pay for an inspection? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The lower-right 80 and lower-left 100 at m: the lower-right should equal the vertically opposite upper-left 72 and the lower-left should equal the upper-right 108. (b) 72 and 108. (c) The angles are 70 and 110 at l, 72 and 108 at m: four different measures. (d) Order the inspection. The directly read corresponding angles differ by 72 - 70 = 2 degrees and 110 - 108 = 2 degrees, which is more than her limit of 1 degree. A gap of 2 is smaller than the 3 degree error of the set square, so the readings cannot show whether the pipes are parallel or not. Paying ₹1,500 is small against the ₹30,000 risk of a crooked backdrop.
s: Part (a): names 80 and 100 as wrong with the vertically opposite reasons
Part (b): corrects them to 72 and 108
Part (c): says four different measures (70, 110, 72, 108)
Part (d): gaps of 2 degrees exceed the 1 degree rule and are within the 3 degree reading error, so orders the ₹1,500 inspection rather than risk ₹30,000

questions.q: A transversal cuts two lines. At the first crossing the lower-right angle is 105 degrees, and at the second crossing the lower-right angle is also 105 degrees. How many of the eight angles must measure 75 degrees?
questions.a: At each crossing the lower-right angle of 105 degrees forms a linear pair with the upper-right and the lower-left angles, so those are 75 degrees; the upper-left angle is vertically opposite and is 105 degrees. That gives 2 angles of 75 degrees at each crossing, 4 in all.

questions.q: Transversal t crosses line l at P and line m at Q, with m below l. Around P the angles are 1 (upper-left), 2 (upper-right), 3 (lower-right) and 4 (lower-left). Around Q the angles are 5 (upper-left), 6 (upper-right), 7 (lower-right) and 8 (lower-left). A student writes the angles as: angle 1 = 110, angle 2 = 70, angle 3 = 70, angle 4 = 110, angle 5 = 70, angle 6 = 110, angle 7 = 110, angle 8 = 70 degrees. Angles 1, 2, 5 and 6 were read with a protractor; angles 3, 4, 7 and 8 were worked out in a hurry. Check the list against the rules for angles at a crossing, find every wrong entry with the reason, write the corrected list, and say what the list tells you about lines l and m.
questions.a: At P the rules are: angle 1 = angle 3, angle 2 = angle 4, and angle 1 + angle 2 = 180. Since angles 1, 2, 5 and 6 were read directly, the hurried entries are the ones to correct. Angle 3 is wrongly 70 (it should equal angle 1 = 110) and angle 4 is wrongly 110 (it should equal angle 2 = 70). At Q the same rules show angle 7 is wrongly 110 (it should equal angle 5 = 70) and angle 8 is wrongly 70 (it should equal angle 6 = 110). Corrected: at P 110, 70, 110, 70; at Q 70, 110, 70, 110. There are two different measures. Corresponding angles 1 and 5 are 110 and 70, not equal, so l and m are not parallel.
s: Applies the rules at P and finds angles 3 and 4 wrong
Applies the rules at Q and finds angles 7 and 8 wrong
Writes the corrected list
Says two different measures
Concludes not parallel because angles 1 and 5 are unequal

questions.q: A student lists the angles made by a transversal in the order upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, lower-left. At the first crossing: 70, 110, 70, 110. At the second crossing: 70, 110, 70, 100. Show that the readings at the second crossing cannot all be right.
questions.a: At the second crossing the lower-left angle should be vertically opposite the upper-right angle, so it must equal 110 degrees, not 100. Also the lower-right angle 70 and lower-left angle 100 form a linear pair and add to 170, not 180. So the readings are impossible.
s: Compares the lower-left angle with its vertically opposite angle 110
Tests the linear pair 70 + 100 = 170, not 180
Concludes the readings at the second crossing cannot all be right

questions.q: A path t crosses two fences l and m, and nobody knows whether the fences are parallel. A surveyor wants all eight angles. What is the smallest number of angles he must actually measure with a protractor?
questions.a: One angle at each crossing is enough: the other three at that crossing follow from linear pairs and vertically opposite angles. One angle alone cannot fix the second crossing unless the fences are known to be parallel.

questions.q:
A town planner in Pune studies a straight road t that crosses two straight rail lines l and m. Around the crossing with l, the upper-left angle is 56 degrees. Around the crossing with m, the lower-right angle is 124 degrees. The planner wants l and m to be parallel for a level-crossing design.
(a) List the four angles around the crossing with l. (b) List the four angles around the crossing with m. (c) How many different measures are there in all, and are the corresponding upper-left angles equal? (d) What must the upper-left angle at m be for the lines to be parallel? By how many degrees must m be turned, and by how many would l have to be turned instead?
questions.a: (a) 56, 124, 56, 124 degrees (upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, lower-left). (b) The lower-right angle 124 gives upper-left 124 (vertically opposite), upper-right and lower-left 56 each. (c) Two different measures, 56 and 124, but the upper-left angles are 56 and 124, not equal. (d) The upper-left angle at m must be 56 degrees (equal to that at l). Its upper-left angle must change from 124 to 56, so m must turn 68 degrees; alternatively l would have to turn 68 degrees the other way, so that its upper-left angle becomes 124.
s: Part (c): says two measures and corresponding angles 56 and 124 are unequal
Part (d): says 56 is needed, so m turns 68 degrees (or l turns 68 degrees the other way)

questions.q: A transversal crosses l and m. At the crossing with l the lower-right angle is 100 degrees and the upper-left angle is (x + 55) degrees; the upper-right angle is 4y degrees. At the crossing with m the upper-left angle is 100 degrees. Find x, find y, then write all eight angles and say how many different measures there are.
questions.a: The upper-left angle at l is vertically opposite the lower-right angle, so x + 55 = 100 and x = 45. The upper-right angle forms a linear pair with it, so it is 80 degrees and 4y = 80 gives y = 20. The angles at l are 100, 80, 100, 80; at m, with upper-left 100, they are 100, 80, 100, 80. There are only two different measures, 100 and 80.
s: Finds x = 45 using vertically opposite angles and y = 20 from 4y = 80
Writes all eight angles
States two different measures

questions.q: A transversal cuts two parallel lines l and m. The upper-left angle at l is (3x + 10) degrees and the upper-left angle at m is (5x - 30) degrees. (a) Find x and the upper-left angle. (b) Find the upper-right angle at m and the lower-right angle at l.
questions.a: (a) Corresponding angles of parallel lines are equal, so 3x + 10 = 5x - 30, giving x = 20 and each upper-left angle is 70 degrees. (b) The upper-right angle at m forms a linear pair with the upper-left angle there: 180 - 70 = 110 degrees. The lower-right angle at l is vertically opposite the upper-left angle at l, so it is 70 degrees.
s: Part (a): equates 3x + 10 and 5x - 30, x = 20, angle 70 degrees
Part (b): 110 degrees for the upper-right angle at m and 70 degrees for the lower-right angle at l

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A transversal on two lines forms eight angles with at most four different measures.
Reason (R): Corresponding angles formed by a transversal on any two lines are always equal.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A transversal cuts two parallel lines l and m. Meera says: 'All four angles at l are equal to all four angles at m.' (a) Which angle at m is equal to the upper-left angle at l, and why? (b) For what transversal is Meera's statement true? Give the measure of the angles.
questions.a: (a) The upper-left angle at m, because corresponding angles of parallel lines are equal. (b) Only when the transversal is perpendicular to the lines: then every angle at both lines is 90 degrees. Otherwise each line has two different measures (such as 65 and 115), so not all four angles at one line are equal.
s: Part (a): the upper-left angle at m, as corresponding angles
Part (b): true only for a perpendicular transversal, all angles 90 degrees

questions.q: True or False: If a transversal makes eight angles that show exactly four different measures, then the two lines it cuts must be parallel. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Four different measures is the most that any two lines can show, because the four pairs of vertically opposite angles are equal. For example 40 and 140 at l with 60 and 120 at m give four measures although the lines are not parallel.
s: Verdict False
Reason: four distinct measures is the maximum for any two lines; example with unequal corresponding angles

questions.q:

Part (b): gets 68 degrees for both rails
